strengths: Addresses an important NLP problem: measuring human contribution in collaborative writing beyond binary AI-text detection. The information-gain perspective provides a concrete, testable starting point.

The evaluation has substantial breadth: four domains with 2,000 source items each, five generations per prompt, multiple generators and scorers, and 2,500 WildChat examples. Results support the broad ordering from polishing to generation using shorter prompts.
The measure is simple, requires no task-specific training, and can evaluate closed-model outputs through surrogate scoring when the original prompts are available.

The high-level presentation is clear. Public dataset and code links are provided, and the discussion acknowledges limitations involving trusted inputs, single-turn interactions, and copyright interpretation.
weaknesses: The central interpretation as a percentage of human contribution lacks adequate theoretical justification. Equations (1)–(3) use a pointwise log-likelihood ratio, rather than expected mutual information. No joint input/output distribution establishes that the no-prompt likelihood is the required output marginal. Furthermore, the normalized score can be negative, as Figures 3, 5, and 6 demonstrate. These properties undermine the nonnegative shared-information interpretation illustrated in Figure 1.

The experiments establish coarse category ordering but do not validate quantitative attribution. Prompt categories simultaneously vary input length, source-text overlap, and semantic detail. There are no length-ratio, lexical-overlap, or semantic-similarity baselines, nor matched controls establishing what the proposed measure adds. WildChat category labels and selected examples provide no independent validation of individual contribution estimates. The acknowledged absence of absolute ground truth does not remove the need for stronger construct validation.

Surrogate-model generalization is supported only at the level of broad ordering. Figure 5 shows substantial changes in scores for the same generated outputs when the evaluator changes; Llama-3 title/subject generations receive negative median scores under Mixtral. Agreement and calibration across scorers need investigation before these values can support transferable percentage estimates.

Reproducibility is insufficiently documented in the supplied PDF. Sampling procedures and prompt templates are deferred to supplementary material that is absent from the provided manuscript. Exact model checkpoints and operational details for unconditional versus conditional likelihood scoring, including chat formatting and output-token treatment, are also unspecified. The public code link is helpful, but these omissions limit assessment of the submitted methodology.

The robustness evidence covers only two fixed prompt additions: using uncommon words and mimicking human writing. Without a defined attack budget, success criterion, or search against the actual score, these experiments support stability under the tested perturbations rather than broad resilience to adaptive attacks.
